The names of the messengers and the exact location differ across the reports, and Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di consider such details of no benefit. The commentators agree that the story is an example offered to the Quraysh so that they may learn from it.

This verse from Surah Ya-Sin gives the reply of the messengers when the people of the town accused them of being mere humans and liars. They said that their Lord knows they are truthful in claiming to be sent to the people, and that their only duty is to deliver the message clearly and plainly; guidance and acceptance are not up to them. Most commentators identify the town as Antioch. They report that two messengers were sent first and then strengthened by a third, but names and details vary between transmitters, and most do not settle on one. All agree that the people's words 'you are only humans like us' amount to a denial of the mission, and that 'our Lord knows' works like an oath to reinforce the assertion. The commentators differ on who sent the messengers. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir hold that God sent them, while al-Qurtubi and Ibn al-Jawzi also report that Jesus sent them, a view that still traces the mission to God as the messengers of His messenger. Al-Razi explains that 'the clear message' may mean distinguishing truth from falsehood through miracle and proof, or making the truth manifest by every possible means. In the following verses, the commentators relate that the people took the arrival of the messengers as a bad omen when rain was withheld, and the messengers replied that the omen lies with the people themselves, because of their disbelief. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi also report that the man who came from the far end of the city, Habib the carpenter, was killed after declaring his faith.

The verse reports the people of the town telling their messengers, after rejecting them, that they see them as a bad omen, and threatening to stone them and inflict painful punishment if they do not stop. The commentators explain tatayyur as taking a bad omen. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Qatada report that rain had been withheld from the town and the people blamed the messengers, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi say ignorant people call good what pleases them and bad what repels them. On the meaning of stoning, Qatada keeps it literal, al-Farra' and others take it to mean killing, and Mujahid and some others take it to mean insulting. The messengers reply that the bad omen is with them, through their own disbelief and deeds, as Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak say, the portion of good and evil that is theirs. Ibn Kathir and Qatada read the following question as a rebuke for threatening those who remind them of God. The scholars differ over who the messengers were: al-Tabari and al-Sam'ani say they were sent by 'Isa, while al-Baghawi and al-Baydawi say they were sent by God. All agree the threat is real and that the misfortune comes from their own disbelief.

The commentators explain that the people of the town tell the messengers, "We see you as a bad omen," meaning they blame the messengers for their misfortune. Al-Tabari, citing Qatada, and Ibn Kathir report that they attribute drought or calamity to the messengers and threaten to stone them and to inflict a painful punishment unless they stop. Nearly all agree that the reply, "Your omen is with you," means that the evil comes from their own disbelief and deeds and not from the messengers. Qatada understands it as their works, Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak as their share of good and evil, and al-Farra' as their provision and actions. Regarding "Because you were reminded," al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Ibn 'Atiyya note that the answer is omitted and the question is a rebuke, while Ibn Kathir takes it as: do you threaten us because we reminded you of God? The readings of the two hamzas and of the verb vary, and the commentators say the meaning stays broadly the same. The word musrifun is explained by Qatada as excessive in their augury, by Yahya ibn Sallam as excessive in disbelief, by Ibn Bahr as corrupters, and by the majority as transgressing the limits. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi also relate the story of Habib the carpenter, who came running from the far end of the city to urge his people to follow the messengers and was killed by them. The tafsirs agree in describing people who see the callers as a bad omen and answer them with threats.

The verse describes a believing man who came running from the far end of the city to urge his people to follow the messengers, who ask no wage and are rightly guided. The commentators differ on his identity and trade. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, Mujahid and 'Ikrima name him Habib the carpenter, al-Suddi says he was a fuller, and 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Hakam says a cobbler. Wahb ibn Munabbih reports that he suffered from leprosy and divided his earnings, feeding his family with half and giving the other half in charity. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi transmit these accounts, while al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi emphasise his faith and sincerity. On the location, al-Tha'alibi, al-Baydawi and Ibn 'Ashur identify the city as Antioch, whereas Ibn Kathir and al-Jaza'iri do not specify it. All report that his people killed him, but they differ on how: Ibn Mas'ud says they trampled him, al-Suddi that they stoned him, and al-Hasan that they hanged him. Regarding his words "fasma'un", al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take them as addressed to his people, while Ibn Mas'ud and al-Qurtubi understand them as a call on the messengers to bear witness to his faith. The commentators mainly draw the lesson of sincere counsel offered to others, even at the cost of one's life.

This passage of Surah Ya-Sin tells of the believing man who came running from the far end of the city to urge his people to follow the messengers, saying: follow those who ask you for no wage and who are rightly guided. The commentators explain that the messengers sought neither money nor status for their message, and that their guidance is a sign of the truth of their call. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Baydawi and al-Qurtubi agree in identifying this man as Habib the carpenter, and that the messengers asked no reward, which is a mark of the caller's sincerity. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi read it as an invitation to follow and a denial of any worldly interest in the one who summons. Ibn Ashur notes that faith often appears at the edges of a town before its centre, where the powerful are more inclined to resist. Al-Tabari and al-Baghawi report that the man was sick or a worshipper in a cave, accounts these authors transmit without firm preference. Al-Mawardi lists several trades attributed to him, including carpenter, cobbler and fuller. Al-Razi explains that the speech moves from the command to follow to the reason for doing so, namely the evident guidance of the messengers. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Atiyya report that he was killed after declaring his faith, and al-Qurtubi notes that the most apparent meaning is that he entered Paradise after his death, while the disagreements about his killing and his entry into Paradise are well known. The commentators do not decide among these views beyond what the text itself allows.

This verse records the words of the believing man who came from the far end of the city, usually identified as Habib the carpenter, as he addresses his people: why should I not worship the One who created me, and to whom you will all be returned? The commentators explain that he attributes the creation to himself because it is a blessing that calls for gratitude, and the return to them because it carries a warning. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi report that he then rejects idol worship: they cannot intercede for him if the Most Merciful wills him harm, nor rescue him from it, and worshipping them would be manifest error. On the phrase 'I have believed in your Lord, so listen to me,' opinions differ. Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Ka'b and Wahb, as transmitted by al-Tabari and Ibn al-Jawzi, take it as addressed to his people, while others, including al-Mawardi and Ibn Kathir, take it as addressed to the messengers so that they may bear witness to his faith. The exegetes agree that his people killed him, but differ on how: stoning while he prayed for them, trampling, or other means. He is then told to enter Paradise, and he wishes his people could know what earned him his Lord's forgiveness. Commentators give two readings of this wish: that they would learn of his good end and believe, or that they would feel regret for their conduct.

The commentators explain that this speech belongs to the believing man of Antioch, who came running to support the messengers. He asks his people why he should not worship the One who created him and to whom they will all return, then rejects taking gods besides God: they cannot ward off a harm that the Most Merciful wills for him, nor rescue him from it, and taking them as gods would be clear error. The exegetes agree that this is an open declaration of divine oneness and sincere counsel to his people. The thing interceded for, according to Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn 'Atiyya, refers to the idols to which the polytheists attributed intercession, and they have no real intercession at all. The disagreement concerns the addressee of the phrase 'I have believed in your Lord, so listen to me'. Ibn 'Abbas, Ka'b and Wahb, followed by Ibn Ishaq and al-Tabari, take it as addressed to his people, while others, including Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Juzayy and al-Baydawi, take it as addressed to the messengers so that they may bear witness for him. Regarding his death, Qatada reports that he was stoned while praying for his people's guidance, and Ibn Mas'ud reports that they trampled him to death; al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir also mention varying accounts of his burial place. All read the words 'Enter Paradise' as the announcement of his reward after death, and his wish that his people knew what earned him forgiveness as evidence that he counselled them even after dying. Al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Atiyya also note the grammatical point about 'ma' in 'bi-ma ghafara li', taken as a verbal noun by most and as an interrogative by al-Farra'.

In this verse the believing man of the city declares that if he were to worship other gods besides God, he would be in clear error. The commentators first explain the plain sense: he sees no reason not to worship the Creator who brought him into being and to whom all will return, and he refuses to take as gods idols that can neither intercede usefully nor save from harm. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi report that he was called Habib al-Najjar and that he hurried from the far end of the city to urge his people to follow the messengers, who ask no wage and are rightly guided.

Opinions differ on who is addressed by the words "I have believed in your Lord, so listen to me." Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Ishaq, among others, take it as addressed to the messengers, asking them to bear witness to his faith, whereas Ibn 'Abbas, Ka'b and Wahb take it as addressed to his own people, to make them aware that he now believes in the Lord they rejected. The accounts of how he was killed vary: Qatada and al-Suddi mention stoning, Ibn Mas'ud mentions being trampled, and others give different traditions. All agree that he was told to enter Paradise and that he wished his people could know of the forgiveness granted him, which al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir read as evidence of his sincere counsel to them even after his death.

This verse records the believing man from the far end of the city declaring his faith in their Lord and asking them to listen. The commentators explain that he had first asked his people why he should not worship the One who created him and to whom they will all return, then rejected taking other gods that could neither intercede nor rescue from harm if the Merciful willed it, calling such a choice clear error. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya report that after these words the people rushed at him as one man and killed him, some saying they stoned him while he prayed for his people, others that they trampled him. The commentators differ on who is addressed by 'so listen to me': Ibn 'Abbas, Ka'b and Wahb say it is his own people, whom he is warning; Ibn Mas'ud and others say it is the messengers, whom he asks to bear witness to his faith; al-Razi and Abu Hayyan also mention that it could address the listeners in general. On 'enter the Garden', al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir relate that it was said to him after death, while Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baydawi take it as a announcement of his admission. His wish 'if only my people knew' is explained as a wish that they learn of his forgiveness and honour so they would believe, or that they would regret their deed. The commentators agree that he remained a sincere adviser to his people, both in life and after death.

This passage describes the death of the believing man Habib the carpenter, who came from the far end of the city urging his people to follow the messengers and then declared his own faith, and was killed for it. He is told to enter the Garden, and he wishes that his people could know what his Lord has forgiven him and how He has honoured him, so that they might believe as he did. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi agree that he was killed and that his entry into Paradise was an honour, like that of the martyrs. They differ on the meaning of the command: Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Ka'b and Wahb take it as a announcement that he had earned Paradise, while Qatada and al-Hasan report that God raised him there alive to be provided for. Al-Razi allows that the words came either after his death or right after his declaration of faith. On the wish, most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari, read it as a hope that his people would learn of his good end and turn to faith, while al-Mawardi also mentions a wish that they become like him; Ibn Abbas says he advised his people both while alive and after death. Al-Zamakhshari draws from the story a lesson on restraining anger and showing forbearance toward the ignorant. Most read the particle in the phrase about forgiveness as a verbal noun, meaning by my Lord's forgiveness, though al-Farra took it as an interrogative.

This passage reports that the believing man of the city, after being killed for urging his people to follow the messengers, was told: "Enter Paradise." He then wished that his people might know what his Lord had forgiven him and how He had honoured him, so that they would believe and attain his state. The commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Juzayy, agree that the forgiveness concerns his sins, granted for his faith and patience, and that the honour means entering Paradise or having his deeds accepted. They report that he counselled his people both while alive and after death, and cite the hadith mentioning him.

Most hold that "Enter Paradise" is a command of honour and good tidings, given after his death, as al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi relate. Al-Mawardi, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi see it rather as an announcement that he deserved Paradise, or as an entry that preceded his death. Al-Hasan says God raised him alive to heaven, while Qatada reports that he lives in Paradise, being provided for, like the martyrs. The majority holds that he was stoned, trampled or killed in other ways that the exegetes mention.

Opinions differ on the meaning of his wish. Al-Mawardi, Ibn Juzayy and al-Zamakhshari hold that he wished his people to know his good end so they would follow him in faith, while others think he wished them to repent and feel regret. As for "ma" in "bima ghafara li", most take it as a verbal particle meaning "by the forgiveness of my Lord". Al-Farra' and al-Zamakhshari allowed an interrogative sense, and others a relative sense, all of which the exegetes accept.

The commentators explain that God states He did not send down on the people of the believing man, after they killed him for calling them to faith, any army from the heavens, because none was needed: a single cry destroyed them, and they became silent and extinguished like embers. Scholars differ on the meaning of 'jund' (host). Mujahid and Qatada take it to mean that no further messenger or prophet was sent after his death, since a prophetic mission is not called an army; al-Tabari holds that God sent no troops to fight them and destroyed them with one cry, and he judges this reading the more sound. Al-Hasan identifies the host as the angels who bring revelation to the prophets, while Ibn Mas'ud reports that God was angered on his servant's behalf and hastened their punishment. On the cry, some say it was the punishment itself, others that it was a cry from Gabriel. The reading 'sayhatun' in the nominative, attributed to Abu Ja'far, is debated: some grammarians consider it weak, while others justify it by giving 'kana' the sense of 'occur'. Several note that sending heavenly hosts, as at Badr or the Trench, was a special honour for the Prophet ﷺ. The passage closes with a warning that mocking the messengers brings lasting regret on the Day of Judgement.

This verse says that the people who killed the man who called to the worship of God were not destroyed by an army sent from heaven, for none was needed; a single cry struck them, and they lay dead and still, like embers gone out. The commentators agree that the cry was the means of their destruction, but they differ on who uttered it. Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi report that it was Gabriel, while al-Jaza'iri and Ibn 'Uthaymin decline to name him, since the text does not do so. On the word "jund" (host), al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya record two readings. Mujahid and Qatada take it to mean a further prophetic message, which God did not send after the killing, while al-Hasan takes it to mean the angels who bring revelation. Al-Tabari prefers the second view, that no heavenly host was needed at all. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan explain that God settles the end of each people in a way that wisdom requires, and that the armies sent at Badr and the Trench honoured the Prophet ﷺ. Abu Ja'far read the word for cry in the nominative, which Abu Hatim and several grammarians rejected on grounds of gender, though others considered it sound. On "Ya hasrata 'ala al-'ibad", Ibn 'Abbas took it as a cry of woe, Abu al-'Aliya and others took it as the regret of the unbelievers, angels, or messengers, and some, such as Abu Hayyan and al-Biqa'i, read it as an expression of the gravity of their sin. Several scholars connect the passage to a warning to the Quraysh, who might suffer the same fate.

This verse expresses intense anguish and regret over those who mocked every messenger sent to them. The commentators treat the address to regret as a figurative device that magnifies the matter and signals that this is the time for it to appear. Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Baghawi and al-Sam'ani explain 'O regret for the servants' as the regret of the servants over themselves, which will come on the Day of Resurrection or when they witness the punishment. Abu al-'Aliya and al-Baghawi relate that the speakers are the doomed themselves, who, on seeing the torment, wish they had believed when it no longer helps them. Al-Dahhak attributes the regret to the angels over the disbelievers who denied the messengers. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir read it as the servants' regret over their own souls for neglecting God's command. Al-Razi and Abu Hayyan note that the article in 'al-'ibad' may refer to a known group or to the category of deniers, that the subject of the regret may remain unstated, and that the address is figurative. Some readers recited 'yā ḥasrata al-'ibād' in the construct form, others 'yā ḥasratā'. Ibn 'Abbas glosses the address as woe. The cause of the regret is the mockery of the messengers. Al-Razi compares it to a man who scorns a visiting king and then discovers his majesty, which brings extreme remorse. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi allow that the regret may come from the angels and the believers, or from God by metaphor, to magnify their offence. The prevailing reading is that mockery is the source of remorse, and the passage then recalls the fate of earlier generations and the gathering of all before God.

This verse recalls that God destroyed many generations before the Quraysh, that they never return to this world, and it calls the deniers to take warning from their fate. The commentators read the question as a rhetorical reminder with rebuke, and take the verb 'to see' to mean 'to know'. Most, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Baydawi, take the address to the people of Mecca and to all who called the messengers liars. They explain that 'that they do not return to them' is an apposition to 'how many We destroyed', meaning: have they not seen the vastness of Our destruction and that they do not come back? Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan specify that this apposition works on the meaning rather than the wording. Al-Farra' instead makes 'how many' depend on the verb 'see'. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi note that Ibn Mas'ud's reading, 'those whom We destroyed', makes it an apposition of inclusion, and that the verse refutes those who believe in a return before the Day of Judgment. On 'all of them shall be brought before Us', the commentators agree it means that all creatures will be assembled for judgment on the Day of Resurrection, though they differ on the sense of 'brought': punished according to as-Suddi, raised up according to Yahya ibn Sallam. The readings of 'lamma' also differ: most read it lightly, while 'Asim, Hamza and Ibn 'Amir read it with emphasis; al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi explain that the emphatic form means 'except', and the light form has an emphatic 'ma'. Both readings, they say, carry closely related meanings.

The commentators explain that this verse follows a reminder to the Meccans that the past generations Allah destroyed will not return to this world. It then states that all creatures will be gathered and brought before Allah on the Day of Resurrection to be judged and recompensed. They agree that the meaning is assembly and presentation for reckoning. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that 'kull' refers to every individual without exception, while 'jami'' refers to their being gathered together; this is why both words are used, a point also noted by al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Ibn 'Ashur. On the word 'muhdarun', al-Suddi takes it to mean those punished, Yahya ibn Sallam those resurrected, and Qatada those mustered, while most hold that it means being brought for the reckoning. On the reading, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that the reading 'lamma' with shadda, followed by Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim and Hamza, and the reading with takhfif, followed by most, yield two meanings: in the first, 'in' is negative and 'lamma' means 'illa'; in the second, 'in' is the lightened form and 'ma' is an emphatic particle. Al-Tabari considers both readings sound and close in meaning. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi observe that the verse teaches that the one Allah destroys is not left without account, since death is not the end.

The commentators explain that the verse speaks of dry, barren land with no vegetation which, once rain falls on it, produces grain that people eat. This sign is taken as proof of God's power to bring the dead back to life after their death, a point on which al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Ashur agree. All of them place the verse within the argument for resurrection, and all recognise that grain is the staple food, as the word order of the text shows. The main disagreement concerns grammar: al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi treat "We gave it life" as a qualifier of the earth or as a clarification of the sign, while Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan take it as an independent explanatory clause, and al-Razi holds that mentioning the grain completes the idea of life. As for "what their hands made", there are two readings. Al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi take it as meaning "that which" or a verbal noun, so that it refers to what people planted and worked, whereas al-Dahhak, Muqatil, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir read it as a negation, the fruit being God's alone. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi explain why palm trees and vines are singled out by their nourishment and usefulness. Most commentators hold that the verse addresses the pagans of Mecca who denied the resurrection. The reference of the pronoun in "its fruit" is also debated, being taken to mean the water, the palm trees, or the gardens mentioned.

This verse recalls that God made, in the earth brought back to life by rain, gardens of palms and vines and caused springs to gush forth, so that people may eat of their fruit, a blessing that calls for gratitude. The commentators agree that it is a sign of God's power and evidence for resurrection after death. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that God caused these fruits to grow as provision for them, while al-Kalbi, al-Farra' and Ibn Qutayba read «ma» in «what their hands made» as meaning «that which», so the fruit was partly the work of human hands. Al-Dahhak and Muqatil take it as a negation: their hands did not make it, they found it already produced. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi note the readings, some reading «'amilathu» with a pronoun and others «'amilat» without one. Al-Razi observes that the palm is singled out for its sweetness and usefulness, and that the springs show God's power to bring water up from high places. Al-Baydawi and Ibn Kathir link the closing mention of the pairs created, from plants, from humans and from what they do not know, to the glorification of God. Ibn 'Ashur holds that the pronoun in «its fruit» refers to the gardens just mentioned, while others refer it to the water or to the palm alone.

In this verse God shows that the dead earth He revives with rain is a sign for the people of Mecca, a proof of His power and of resurrection. From it He brings forth grain that sustains them, and He places in it gardens of palm and grapevines along with flowing springs. The commentators agree that the purpose of this provision is that people eat of its fruit, but they differ on what the pronoun in « its fruit » refers to. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn 'Atiyya take it to refer to what was just mentioned, namely the gardens, the palms and the vines, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi take it to refer back to God through a shift of grammatical person, and Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi note further possibilities such as the water. As for « what their hands made », most read « ma » as a relative clause linked to the fruit, meaning what people process or cultivate, such as grape juice or date syrup. Al-Dahhak, Muqatil and, in one reading, Ibn Kathir take « ma » as a negation: the fruit was not made by human hands but is God's creation. The verse ends by rebuking people for their lack of gratitude and then glorifies the One who created all kinds of pairs, from what the earth grows, from human beings, and from things beyond human knowledge.

This passage of Surah Yasin, following the mention of the dead earth that God revives and the grain, fruits and springs He brings forth from it, declares God free of any partner. He is the One who created all pairs: what the earth grows, males and females among humans, and other things that people do not know. Most commentators read the phrase as a glorification that rejects polytheism, pointing to God's power to raise the dead and to the duty to be grateful to Him. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi take 'pairs' to mean kinds and species, and 'from themselves' to mean male and female. They understand 'what they do not know' as creatures and realities that God has not revealed to people, while Ibn 'Ashur includes the secrets of creation, such as the soul. Al-Razi observes that the wording is general and covers human acts, which are also created by God. Opinions differ, however, on the meaning of 'ma' in 'and what their hands have made'. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir read it as a relative pronoun, meaning what they planted and cultivated, whereas Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak and Muqatil, as reported by Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Kathir, read it as a negation, so that the fruit is solely God's work. The recitations also differ over whether the pronoun is included. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi explain that 'glory be to Him' expresses astonishment at the disbelief of the polytheists despite the blessings they see. Most commentators agree that the verse affirms the oneness of the Creator.

This passage presents a sign of God's power: night arrives when the light of day is withdrawn from it, and people are suddenly plunged into darkness. Commentators explain that "naslakh" means to strip away, as the skin is stripped from a sheep, and that "minhu" means "from it" in the sense of "away from it." Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi note that darkness is the original state and day is what comes upon it, while Ibn 'Atiyya considers this inference open to question. As for the sun, most say it runs toward its resting place, and opinions differ on what that place is. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi cite the hadith of Abu Dharr, transmitted by al-Bukhari and Muslim, placing it beneath the Throne. Ibn Kathir takes it as a fixed place and also mentions a fixed time. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya understand it as the extreme points of its risings and settings through the seasons, Qatada as a single appointed term it never exceeds, and others as the Day of Resurrection when it is folded up. Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas read "there is no resting place for it," meaning perpetual motion. The commentators then turn to the moon and its twenty-eight stations, its return like an old palm frond, the sun's inability to overtake the moon and the night's inability to outrun the day, each floating in its orbit. All agree that these verses are proofs of God's power and knowledge, even though they differ on the details of the resting place and the orbit.

The commentators explain that this verse belongs to the signs that show God's power: the sun runs its course toward a fixed resting place that God has ordained, which it neither exceeds nor falls short of, and this is the decree of the Almighty, the All-Knowing. Most agree that this motion is constant and never ceases, and that the verse reminds us of the precise order of creation. They differ, however, on what this resting place is. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and others take it as a physical place beneath the Throne, relying on the hadith of Abu Dhar transmitted by al-Bukhari and Muslim, where the sun prostrates and asks permission to return, which is granted. Qatada, Mujahid and Ibn Qutayba understand it as the furthest limit of its risings and settings, or as an appointed term, some linking it to the end of this world and the coming of the Hour. Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas recited it as "there is no resting place for it", meaning it never stops moving. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi set out further readings, distinguishing a temporal from a spatial rest and tying the motion to the orbit that carries it. Al-Alusi notes that several scholars keep the hadith on its apparent sense while remaining cautious in explaining it. Most commentators do not choose between these opinions and treat them together as facets of the meaning.

The commentators explain that the verse speaks of the moon, which God measured in stations that it traverses each month: it first appears as a thin crescent, grows to a full moon, then wanes until at the end of the month it returns like a dried, curved palm-bunch stalk. Nearly all agree that the arjun is the stalk of the date cluster that bears the small branches, and that when it dries and ages it becomes thin, bent and yellowish; the moon is compared to it in its slenderness, curvature and colour. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi add other senses of the word "old" and note that antiquity need not mean a year. On the reading, Ibn Kathir, Abu Hayyan and others report that "the moon" may be read in the nominative (Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr) or accusative (the Kufans and Ibn 'Amir), both being valid according to al-Tabari. The stations number twenty-eight, whose names al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Abbas give, the moon passing through one each night. On the sun and night, Mujahid and Qatada say each has its own domain and does not encroach upon the other; Ibn 'Abbas says one passes before the other when they meet; al-Hasan says they do not meet on the night of the crescent. Al-Zamakhshari explains that the sun cannot overtake the moon because of its slowness and the moon cannot precede the day because of its speed, whereas Ibn 'Atiyya holds that the alternation of day and night is continuous. The hadith of Abu Dhar about the sun's prostration beneath the Throne is cited to explain its course toward a fixed place, while others take it to mean a temporal end on the Day of Resurrection. Ibn Kathir notes finally that the Arabs named the nights of the month according to the state of the moon.

The verse says that the sun, the moon, the night and the day each have a fixed limit set by God that they cannot exceed. The sun cannot overtake the moon to extinguish its light, and the night cannot precede the day to enter before the day has ended. All of them move in an orbit in which they swim. Ibn 'Abbas explains that when they meet in the sky, one is ahead of the other in mansions they do not share, while Mujahid holds that the light of one does not resemble the light of the other. Qatada speaks of each one's authority: when the power of one comes, the power of the other departs. Al-Hasan says they do not meet in the sky only on the night of the new moon, whereas Yahya ibn Sallam restricts this to the night of the full moon, since the moon sets before the sun rises. The word falak is taken by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada to mean a rounded thing like a spindle whorl, and yasbahun to mean moving or revolving. Al-Zamakhshari reads the word sabq as escaping or getting clear, and Ibn 'Ashur reads it similarly. Some commentators drew from the verse a conclusion about whether day or night came first, but Ibn Kathir and others do not accept this reading. The detailed accounts of the shape of the orbits belong to the astronomy of the earlier scholars, and the text does not settle that question.

This verse presents the sea and ships as a sign of God's power. He carried the descendants of those saved in the loaded ark, and He created for them vessels like it that they can ride. Were He to drown them, no one could cry out to save them, but by His mercy He spares them and grants them enjoyment until an appointed term. The commentators broadly agree that the "laden ship" is a full, heavily loaded vessel, that drowning concerns only water, that the "sarikh" is one who answers a cry for help, and that rescue means deliverance from drowning. The main disagreement concerns the word "dhurriyya". Ibn 'Abbas and several others, followed by Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi, take it to mean the ancestors carried in Noah's ark, with their descendants still in their loins. Al-Suddi, Ibn Atiyya, Ibn al-Jawzi and Muqatil take it as offspring, children or women. Ibn Atiyya rejects the use of the word for ancestors, while al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi link the pronoun to the people of Mecca and their children. On the "like it" that is created, Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Malik, al-Dahhak and Qatada speak of ships built on the same pattern, while al-Hasan, Mujahid and 'Ikrima understand camels, the ships of the desert. Al-Tabari favours ships, since drowning only applies to water, and Ibn al-Qayyim argues that the likeness is between ship and ship. Al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari stress the reminder of blessings, and al-Razi holds that the "ship" names the class of vessels.

This verse reminds the polytheists of God's favour at sea: He carried their offspring in the laden ship, Noah's ark, and created for them the like of it to ride. The commentators differ on two points. As for "their offspring", Ibn 'Abbas and others take it to mean the ancestors saved with Noah, or the children and women carried aboard; 'Ali, as al-Mawardi reports, took it to mean the drops of semen in the wombs, a reading Ibn Kathir does not accept. As for "the like of it", most scholars, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi, understand ships built after Noah's ark, and al-Tabari prefers this view because drowning can only happen at sea. Others, such as al-Hasan, Abd Allah ibn Shaddad and Mujahid, understand camels, which al-Razi and Ibn al-Qayyim find less convincing. All agree on the closing part: if God wished, He would drown them and none could cry for help or rescue them; their deliverance is mercy and enjoyment for a time. Qatada explains that term as death, and Yahya ibn Salam as the Day of Resurrection. The following verses warn the disbelievers about what lies before and behind them, yet they turn away from every sign.

The commentators explain that this verse belongs to a series of signs meant to show God's power and mercy toward people. If He wills, He will drown those aboard the ships, and no one will cry out for them or rescue them from the sea. If they are saved, it is by His mercy, which grants them enjoyment of life for an appointed term. The exegetes agree that the word sarikh means one who gives help, and that the word yunqadhun means being rescued from drowning or from ruin, and that such rescue comes only by God's leave and grace. Ibn Abbas, Qatada and others take the drowning to refer to those in the ships, and the rescue to be a mercy from God. Al-Razi notes that help prevents punishment before it strikes, while rescue removes it after it has come. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya debate whether the exception that follows is disjunctive or restrictive. Qatada understands the term hin to mean death, while Yahya ibn Salam takes it to mean the Day of Resurrection. Ibn Ashur sees in the verse a reminder that a blessing can turn into a trial by God's will, a Qur'anic method that combines promise and warning.

The commentators explain that this verse follows the mention of the ships that carry people across the sea. If God wills, He would drown those aboard, and no one could cry out for them or rescue them from drowning. Only a mercy from God saves them, and grants them enjoyment of life until an appointed term. Most exegetes, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi, take "a mercy from Us" as the reason for the exception, meaning they are saved only by God's mercy. Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Razi and al-Alusi note that the exception may also be read as disjunctive, meaning "but a mercy from Us". As for the term, Qatada understands it as death, Yahya ibn Sallam as the Day of Resurrection, and most others as the end of their lifespans. Al-Razi explains that being saved may mean escaping drowning or punishment. Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Baghawi take the laden ship to be Noah's ark, with the passengers being the ancestors. Other commentators do not reject this reading but do not adopt it either. Al-Tabari concludes that the sense of ships is most fitting, since drowning can occur only on water. Ibn 'Ashur and Ibn 'Uthaymin stress that deliverance does not make a person immortal, since no one can escape death for more than a time.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the disbelievers who, when told to beware of what lies before them and behind them, that is, the punishments God sent upon earlier nations and what awaits in the Hereafter, so that they may be shown mercy, turn away. Al-Tabari adds that the mercy hoped for is granted to those who abandon polytheism and believe. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi agree that the verse is a warning about the consequences of disbelief and that the answer to the conditional clause is omitted, understood as 'they turned away', which the following verse confirms by stating that they turn away from every sign that comes to them. This turning away is presented as their constant habit. On the meaning of 'what is before you and behind you', opinions differ. Mujahid and Ibn Jubayr take it as past and future sins, Qatada and Muqatil as the punishments of earlier nations and the punishment of the Hereafter, and Sufyan as this world and the Hereafter, while the reverse is attributed to Ibn Abbas in another report. Al-Razi lists several possibilities, including sins, kinds of torment, or the Prophet and the Resurrection. Al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud mention heavenly and earthly calamities as well. No commentator decisively prefers one reading, and several treat them as compatible. Ibn Ashur notes that Arabic uses these expressions in both directions, which accounts for the variety of interpretations.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the habit of the Meccan disbelievers, who turned away from every sign of God. No proof of God's oneness or of the Prophet's truthfulness reached them without their turning away from it and refusing to reflect on it. Many exegetes, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Baydawi, hold that the answer to the conditional clause of the previous verse ("when it is said to them: fear…") is omitted and is understood from this verse: they turned away. Al-Tabari adds that their turning away covered every sign, and that this verse stands for both statements. Al-Razi connects the verse to what precedes: when the messengers came, they called them liars, and when signs came, they turned away from them, or else they demanded other miracles.

Opinions differ on the meaning of "what is before you and what is behind you". Mujahid takes it as past and future sins, Qatada as the punishments that befell earlier peoples and the Hour, while Sufyan reverses these, reading it as this world and the next. Al-Mawardi adds a fourth reading, what is visible and what is hidden. On the word "ayah", al-Mawardi reports that it can mean a verse of the Book, a messenger, or a miracle.

Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi note that the first "min" reinforces the negation and the second marks a part, so the sense is that turning away was their constant habit before every sign and every warning. Ibn 'Ashur observes that the passive "qila" is used because the Prophet is the one conveying the divine message. Ibn Sa'di and Ibn 'Uthaymin conclude that this refusal reveals the hardness of their hearts.

This verse reports how the disbelievers respond when they are asked to spend from what God has provided: they say that they will not feed one whom God, if He willed, would feed Himself, and they call the believers' appeal to generosity clear misguidance. The commentators broadly agree on a Meccan setting, though al-Hasan al-Basri takes the speakers to be Jews and Qatada to be zindiqs, while Muqatil and al-Naqqash name the Quraysh who set aside a share of their wealth for their idols. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir read the words as a justification of stinginess through divine will, whereas al-Mawardi also considers a denial that alms are obligatory or a complaint against God enriching whom He enriches. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi see a mockery of believers who attach everything to God's will, and al-Razi argues the claim is empty, since God makes some rich and others poor as a trial, and the wealthy person must give without God needing his money. On the closing phrase, 'you are only in clear error', opinions differ: al-Tabari takes it as the disbelievers' words to the believers and prefers this view, while another reading makes it God's reply to the disbelievers, and Ibn Juzayy and al-Baydawi mention both possibilities. The following verses record the question 'when will this promise come?', which the commentators link to the Resurrection, and the single Cry to the first blast of the trumpet, whose recitation and meaning of 'yakhissimun' the exegetes discuss at length.

This verse records the mocking challenge of the disbelievers, who ask when the promised event will come if the believers are truthful. The commentators agree that it refers to the Resurrection and Judgment, and that the question is asked in scorn and defiance rather than in earnest. Al-Mawardi reports two readings: it may mean the punishment that was threatened, or, according to Qatada, the believers' victory over them. Ibn 'Atiyya notes that the word promise is here used ironically for a threat, since promise normally signals good.

The answer in the following verse is that they await only a single cry that will seize them while they are busy disputing. Most exegetes, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi, identify this cry with the first blast of the trumpet, which strikes people in their markets and affairs, leaving them no time to make a bequest or return to their families. The readings of the word yakhissimun differ among the reciters, and al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir stress that people will be taken unaware.

The general meaning the commentators draw is that the Hour comes suddenly, does not hasten at human demand, and that knowledge of its time belongs to God alone.

The commentators explain that the idolaters who mock God's promise are only waiting for a single cry, the first blast of the Trumpet, which will seize them unawares while they are busy disputing over their affairs. They agree that this cry is the blast of terror or of swooning, which surprises people in their daily life, leaving them no chance to make a bequest or return to their families. Al-Tabari, citing Abdullah ibn Amr and Abu Hurayra, describes people in the markets and gatherings at that moment, and Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn Atiyya give the same sense. The word yakhissimun has been read in several ways, and most exegetes, such as al-Tabari, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Kathir, understand it as quarrelling over worldly matters such as buying and selling. Al-Mawardi and Ibn Atiyya also suggest that they dispute about the resurrection. Al-Zamakhshari says they may think themselves winning the argument. As for the addressees, most hold that they are the Quraysh, and several report occasions of revelation linked to refusing to feed the poor. Al-Razi develops the point that the command to spend includes feeding and other giving. The commentators agree that the verse warns that the Hour will come suddenly, and that death is a resurrection for each person.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the state of the disbelievers when the Hour arrives. They are waiting for nothing but a single cry, the first blast of the Trumpet, which will seize them while they are busy with their disputes and dealings in the markets. They will then be unable to make a bequest or return to their families, but will die where they stand. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi cite traditions from the Prophet ﷺ describing people who are selling, buying, or watering their animals when the cry reaches them. Qatada, quoted by al-Tabari, says they were given no time. The exegetes agree that the cry is the first blast and that the swiftness of death is the central point.

Opinions differ on the phrase "while they dispute". Al-Sudi understands them to be talking about their livelihoods and trade, al-Zamakhshari understands them to be absorbed in their quarrels and unaware of the Hour, and al-Razi notes that the heedless person is more terrified than one who expects it. Some take the dispute to be over the resurrection itself. The recitations vary; al-Tabari, Ibn al-Jawzi and Abu Hayyan hold that they are close in meaning and none should be preferred.

Regarding the inability to make a bequest, Qatada and Muqatil see a haste that overtakes them before any arrangement can be made, while Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi extend it to advising others about property or repentance. On not returning to their families, Qatada takes it as not returning to their homes, Abu Hayyan allows that it may mean not returning to them even in speech, and al-Razi understands it as certainty that they will never go back.

This verse describes the second blast of the Trumpet, the blast of resurrection, when people rise from their graves and hasten toward their Lord. The commentators broadly agree that the graves are the "ajdath" and that "yansilun" means walking swiftly, though Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada gloss it as going out. Al-Mawardi and al-Qurtubi report forty years between the two blasts; some hold that the first is the blast of terror and death, while others, such as al-Qurtubi, argue there are only two blasts. When the people cry out, "Who raised us from our resting place?", Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and Ubayy ibn Ka'b explain that God lifts punishment between the blasts so they rest, while others say the torment of the grave seems like sleep beside the fire of Hell. On who answers "This is what the Merciful promised and the messengers spoke truly", Mujahid and Qatada attribute it to the believers, al-Hasan to the angels, and Ibn Zayd to the disbelievers speaking among themselves. Al-Tabari judges the first view closer to the apparent sense of the text. All agree that a single cry then gathers all creatures for judgment, and that the swift walking does not conflict with the standing and looking mentioned in another verse, since the two moments are close together.

This verse describes what happens at the second blast of the trumpet, the trumpet of resurrection, when people rise from their graves, the ajdath, and hasten toward their Lord. The disbelievers then cry out in regret: 'Woe to us! Who has raised us from our resting place?' The answer is given: 'This is what the Most Merciful promised, and the messengers spoke the truth.' The commentators agree that the trumpet is the trumpet of resurrection, that the verb yansilun means moving swiftly, and that the single cry gathers everyone for judgment. On who speaks the words 'this is what the Merciful promised', al-Tabari, Mujahid and Qatada take them to be the believers answering the disbelievers, al-Hasan takes them to be the angels, and Ibn Zayd takes them to be the disbelievers recalling what the messengers had told them. Al-Tabari prefers the believers, since the disbelievers' question about who woke them shows they do not know the answer, while Ibn Kathir considers the views can be combined. As for the 'resting place', Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan judge the report of a nap between the two blasts to be unreliable and read the phrase as a metaphor, while al-Razi and al-Qurtubi note that the punishment of the grave seems light compared with hell. Al-Zamakhshari reads the answer as deliberately turning away from the question of who raised them, to emphasise the greatness of the great resurrection. The recitations differ on some words, such as as-Sur and al-Ajdath, without much effect on the meaning.

The commentators explain that verse 53 concludes the description of the Day of Resurrection: there will be only one cry, the blast of the trumpet, and all creatures will then be gathered before God for judgment. Ibn Kathir, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi read it as a way of showing how easy resurrection is for God, who needs neither means nor delay. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir understand the blast as the trumpet of resurrection, while Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi recall that there are two blasts, with forty years between them according to a hadith cited by Ibn al-Jawzi. They largely agree that this cry is the trumpet of Israfil. Al-Tabari and Ibn al-Jawzi note the reading difference between the accusative and nominative forms of « sayha »; al-Baydawi and Abu Hayyan explain the nominative as a use of kana in its complete sense. The commentators conclude that the verse affirms God's justice on that day: no soul will be wronged, and each will be repaid only for what they did, as Ibn 'Ashur and Ibn al-Jawzi emphasise. The verse thus ends with the announcement of a general gathering from which no one can escape.

This verse describes the Day of Resurrection, when no soul will be wronged in the least and people will be repaid only for what they did. The commentators explain that no reward for good deeds will be diminished and no one will bear another's burden. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi agree that this repayment is perfectly just, neither exceeding nor falling short, and that the address is to all people. They take it as words spoken to the wrongdoers when they see the punishment, confirming the truth and rebuking them. Al-Razi notes that the denial of injustice reassures the believer, while tying repayment to one's deeds dispels the hopes of the criminal. Al-Zamakhshari and others understand the repayment as being in the very likeness of the deed, while others take it as a rule of kind, so good for good and evil for evil. Ibn 'Ashur reads the opening fa' as a eloquent particle implying an unstated speech, and argues that the absence of injustice means the harsh punishment of the wicked is still fair, since God knows all things. Al-Sa'di adds that whoever finds good should thank God, and whoever finds otherwise should blame only himself. They agree that the verse prepares the description of the people of Paradise that follows, and that divine justice appears here in its completeness.

This verse describes the state of the people of Paradise on the Day of Judgment: they are absorbed in the bliss they enjoy, so that nothing else occupies them, and they live in delight. The commentators give the word for occupation closely related meanings. Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab and Qatada understood it as deflowering the virgins; Ibn 'Abbas is also reported to have said it means the playing of lutes, Waki' said it means listening to music, and Ibn Kaysan said it means mutual visiting among the people of Paradise, while others said it is God's hospitality. Mujahid, al-Hasan and Ibn Kathir took it as the bliss that keeps them from the punishment of the people of the Fire, which al-Tabari favours as a meaning that brings the others together. Al-Kalbi said they are absorbed away from their relatives among the people of the Fire, whom they no longer think about. As for 'fakihun', Ibn 'Abbas explained it as 'joyful', Mujahid and Qatada as 'admiring', al-Hasan and Ibn Kathir as 'living in comfort', while Abu 'Ubayda and al-Kisa'i understood it as 'possessors of fruit'. The variant readings of the vowels in 'shughl' and of 'fakihun' or 'fakihin' are described as dialect forms with close meanings. The verse goes on to say that they and their spouses recline on couches in shade, that they have fruits and whatever they ask for, and that peace is greeted to them by a merciful Lord. Al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir cite the hadith of Jabir about God's appearance who greets them, though Ibn Kathir notes weakness in its chain.

This verse describes the state of the people of Paradise on that day: they and their spouses are in shade, reclining on couches. The commentators agree that the 'arā'ik are couches set inside canopied enclosures, as Mujahid, Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrima, al-Hasan and Qatada state; Tha'lab adds that a couch is not called an arika without its canopy, while Ibn Juzayy and Abu Hayyan note that the word can also mean a simple bed. The word 'zilal' is read as the plural of 'zill' by most readers and as 'zulal' by Hamza and al-Kisa'i. Some say Paradise has no sun and its light resembles the dawn before sunrise, while others understand the shade as sheltering pavilions. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take the spouses to be believing women, whereas many take them to be the houris; al-Razi and al-Alusi allow both to be included. They will have fruits and whatever they desire; al-Tabari, al-Mawardi and Ibn Kathir explain 'yaddda'un' as what they wish for. The greeting 'salam' is understood in different ways: following Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take it as God's own greeting spoken to them, supported by a hadith from Jabir, while others see it as the greeting of the angels. The overall meaning is complete felicity and perfect peace.

This verse from Surah Ya-Sin describes what awaits the people of Paradise on the Day of Judgment: they have abundant and varied fruits there which they enjoy, and whatever they desire and ask for. Most commentators understand "fruit" as something savoured for pleasure rather than for sustenance, and Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Baydawi and al-Alusi note that their eating is not to relieve hunger. The word "yaddaʿūn" is explained by Abu 'Ubayda, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir as "they wish for", while al-Zajjaj takes it as "what they call for, which comes to them", and al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi also allow the sense of claiming: whatever they claim is theirs. As for "salamun qawlan min rabbin rahim", al-Zajjaj makes it a substitute for "what they wish", while others make it a predicate or a subject. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir cite the hadith of Jabir about the Lord greeting the people of Paradise, and the report of Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi about their asking for His pleasure; Ibn Kathir however considers the chain of this report weak. Ibn 'Abbas, according to Ibn Kathir, said that God Himself is peace upon them. The majority reading has "salamun" in the nominative, Ibn Mas'ud's reading "salaman" in the accusative. Finally, "wamtazu al-yawma ayyuha al-mujrimun" means that the wrongdoers are separated from the believers; al-Dahhak says each group of disbelievers has its own dwelling in Hell, and Qatada that they are cut off from all good.

The commentators present this verse as good news for the people of Paradise on the Day of Judgment: they are absorbed in their delights, reclining with their spouses on couches in pleasant shade, they have fruits there and all that they desire, and then peace reaches them from a Lord, Most Merciful. The exegetes agree that God greets them with peace as a mark of honour, and that this greeting is the highest of their wishes. They cite in this regard the hadith of Jabir ibn Abdullah, in which the Lord looks down upon them and says: 'Peace be upon you, people of Paradise,' and they gaze at Him and turn to no delight so long as they keep looking at Him. Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and al-Sa'di report this sense, and Ibn Kathir notes that its chain is questionable. As for the report from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, Ibn Kathir describes it as a strange report. Ibn Abbas, Muqatil and others hold that the angels convey the greeting from their Lord, while others say God grants them safety. Grammarians differ on the role of the word 'salam': al-Zamakhshari makes it an apposition to 'what they ask for', others a subject or predicate, and Ibn Mas'ud reads it in the accusative. Al-Tabari prefers it as the predicate of 'what they ask for', with 'qawlan' rendering what they ask for, relying on the report of Muhammad ibn Ka'b. Al-Razi lays out several possibilities without settling the matter. As for 'qawlan', many take it as an absolute object, meaning God speaks thus, while al-Sha'rawi holds that God Himself is the direct speaker. The commentators treat this greeting as evidence of the divine mercy by which people enter Paradise, as the hadith indicates.

On the Day of Resurrection, God commands the criminals to separate themselves from the believers, a command meant as rebuke and humiliation. The commentators explain it as withdrawal and isolation from the people of Paradise who are led to it. Qatada says they will be cut off from all good, and al-Zajjaj and al-Suddi say they must stand apart. Al-Dahhak reports that every disbeliever will have a dwelling in the Fire where he neither sees nor is seen, so the separation also applies among the disbelievers themselves. Dawud ibn al-Jarrah holds that the Muslims will be set apart from the criminals, except those who follow their desires, who will remain with them.

God then addresses them: Did I not charge you, children of Adam, not to serve Satan, for he is a clear enemy to you, and to serve Me, for this is the straight path? The commentators agree that the covenant is the command conveyed through the prophets, and that serving Satan means obeying him in disobedience to God. Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi relate monotheism to the straight path. Ibn Kathir explains that jibillan means a great multitude, and al-Dahhak says a single jibil is ten thousand.

Readers differed on the vocalisation of jibillan, but all the readings carry the meanings of creation and group. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi present the gathering as a cause of regret, and al-Razi speaks of marks appearing on the criminals' faces. The commentators draw no legal ruling from this passage.

The commentators read this verse as a rebuke addressed to the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection, after they have been told to separate themselves from the believers. They are reproached because God had charged them, through His messengers, not to obey Satan, who is a plain enemy to them. The commentators broadly agree that worshipping Satan here means obeying him in disobedience to God, and that the word worship covers any obedience that involves submission and humility. Al-Tabari, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi explain it as obeying his whisperings and the things he makes attractive, and Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi give the same sense. Al-Mawardi and al-Qurtubi explain that the phrase "a considerable multitude" means a large number of creatures or nations, the meaning most commentators accept, though they note several recitations of the word. On the nature of the covenant there is disagreement: al-Razi and Ibn Kathir take it to be the injunctions conveyed by the prophets, al-Razi also mentions the rational proofs God set in human nature, and others see it as the pact taken from the offspring of Adam. Ibn 'Ashur reads the verse as a condemnation of idolatry and holds that Satan's enmity is evident from the repeated whisperings that lead people to ruin. Al-Razi extends the point to the inner life, arguing that obedience to Satan often starts in the heart through desire before it shows in outward acts.

This verse of Surah Ya-Sin recalls the covenant God made with the children of Adam through the messengers: not to worship Satan, who is their clear enemy, and to worship God alone. Many commentators, including al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir, explain that worship here means obedience, so obeying Satan in disobedience to God is a form of worship of him. As for the phrase "this is the straight path", it refers either to what was enjoined, namely abandoning the worship of Satan and worshipping the Merciful, or to the oneness of God, the correct religion that leads to the goal. Al-Zamakhshari takes the indefinite form of "path" as emphasis, meaning a path perfectly straight, while others, such as al-Alusi, allow that it may denote only part of the straight path, with monotheism being one part of it. Al-Razi develops the idea that the Lawgiver is a physician of souls, forbidding what corrupts and then commanding what heals, and that the straight path is followed because man is a traveller heading toward his Lord. On the word "jibillan", al-Tabari, Mujahid and Qatada take it to mean a great multitude, and Ibn Kathir follows this reading. Some commentators place the verse in the scene of the Day of Judgment, when the wrongdoers are ordered to separate, while others read it as a general address to humanity in this life. Ibn Ashur notes that the worship of Satan includes the worship of the idols to which he calls people.

This verse states that Satan has led astray a great multitude of you, and rebukes the disbelievers for not using their reason to avoid obeying him. The commentators agree that the word jibil means a large multitude, a great number of creatures or peoples, and that the various readings of the word are dialects with the same meaning. According to al-Dahhak, reported by al-Mawardi and al-Qurtubi, a jibil is at least ten thousand, and only God knows the full number. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya understand the verse as addressed to the disbelievers in a tone of reproach, reminding them that obeying Satan brought earlier nations to ruin. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi limit themselves to explaining the readings and their linguistic sense. Al-Razi adds that leading astray means turning people away from the straight path, and that the word jibil suggests gathering. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir also cite hadiths on the Day of Judgment, when mouths are sealed and limbs bear witness. Ibn 'Ashur explains that the enmity of Satan is shown by the harmful results of his whisperings. The commentators do not settle between these readings and leave the choice open to the reader.

The commentators explain that this verse is addressed to the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection, after they have been rebuked for obeying Satan and abandoning the worship of God. They are told that this is the Hell they were warned of in the world and called a lie, and they are commanded to enter it and taste its burning because of their disbelief. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi read it as a reminder of the threat given in this life, and Ibn Kathir stresses that it is a rebuke and reproof. The exegetes agree that "today" refers to the Day of Resurrection, and that the order to burn is a humiliation and punishment rather than a real obligation. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya note that Jahannam is the first tier of the Fire. Al-Razi explains that this reproach intensifies their anguish in three ways: the command is a humiliation, the punishment is now present after the pleasures of life have ended, and disbelief implies a blessing that was denied, so that the shame before the benefactor is a very sharp pain. Al-Qurtubi and al-Baghawi cite the hadith of Anas that after the mouths are sealed the limbs bear witness, and some reports make the thigh the first to speak. Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Baydawi discuss the various readings of the word "jibillan", all meaning creation or a multitude. Ibn 'Uthaymin observes that the word "promised" here carries the sense of a threat, while al-Sha'rawi sees the warning as a kindness that allows one to correct the error. All agree that the phrase "you were warned" means they had been told they would enter the Fire and had treated that warning as a lie.

God tells the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection that this is the Hellfire they were promised in the world, and orders them to enter it and feel its heat because of their disbelief. The commentators generally read the command as humiliation and reproach rather than a real instruction. Al-Tabari explains that it means being burned for denying and rejecting in this life, and Ibn Kathir, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi say much the same. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the ba' indicates cause and that ma is a verbal noun. Most link the verse to the preceding reproach for following Satan, and Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn 'Atiyya note that Jahannam is the first layer of the Fire. Several works cite hadiths about the sealing of mouths and the limbs testifying, as in Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi, and they differ on which limb speaks first, the left thigh in some reports and the right in others. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi list several readings of the word jiblan, meaning creation or community; al-Nahhas prefers the majority reading, though the meaning stays the same. There is broad agreement on the main sense of warning, reproach and the visible presence of the Fire, with no excuse left to the disbeliever. The details about the limbs remain debated, and no view is preferred here.

This verse describes the Day of Resurrection, when God will seal the mouths of the disbelievers so that they cannot speak, while their hands will speak and their feet will bear witness to what they earned of sins in this world. The commentators explain that this happens after the deniers have insisted and sworn that they had not associated partners with God; then their mouths are sealed and their limbs speak. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir cite traditions on this, including the hadith of Anas about a servant addressed by his Lord, and the report of 'Uqba ibn 'Amir that the first limb to speak is the left thigh. Ibn Kathir and Abu al-Su'ud also cite a report from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari that the right thigh speaks first, so the narrations differ on which part begins. On the nature of this speech, Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi hold that the limbs truly speak, a speech God creates in them, whereas al-Alusi and Ibn Sa'di understand it as the evidence that sins leave on those limbs. Razi gives the reason for assigning speech to the hands and testimony to the feet: the hands perform the deeds directly, while the feet are present but do not act, and the words of the doer are an admission while those of the witness are testimony. Al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi and al-Mahalli describe the same scene more briefly. Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn 'Atiyya note variant readings, which do not change the general meaning. Overall, the commentators agree that each limb bears witness to the deeds it performed before God.

This verse says that God, if He willed, would blot out the eyes of the disbelievers so that, even when they hurried toward the path, they could not find their way, just as He had sealed their mouths. The commentators differ on what the blotting out means. Al-Tabari, al-Hasan, Qatada and al-Suddi understand physical blindness, that God would leave them blind and wandering, while Ibn Abbas, Ata and Muqatil understand blindness of the heart, that is, misguidance away from the truth. Most identify the path (sirat) as the road itself, though Ibn Zayd takes it to mean the truth. On the grammar of the verb istabaqa taking its object directly, al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and Ibn Atiyya offer several readings, including the dropping of a preposition and the sense of rushing ahead. On the transformation (maskh) in place, al-Hasan and Qatada speak of the disbelievers being made to stay fixed in their dwellings, Ibn Abbas of their destruction there, al-Suddi of an alteration of their form, and Abu Salih of their turning to stone; Ibn Salam takes the whole warning to refer to the Day of Resurrection. All agree that the verse displays God's complete power and that He restrains it by wisdom. Several also cite the testimony of the limbs on the Day of Judgment, with the sealing of the mouth, relying on narrations transmitted in Muslim and other collections.

The commentators explain that the verse describes a punishment God could inflict on the disbelievers in this world if He willed: blinding them so they cannot find the road, and fixing them in place so they can neither advance nor turn back. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that most read it as a warning to the Quraysh, with the punishment withheld out of mercy and as a respite. Al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud note that the conditional expresses an impossibility, since God's will does not apply. On the meaning of blinding, al-Tabari, al-Hasan and Qatada take it as physical blindness leaving people wandering, while Ibn Abbas, Qatada and Muqatil understand the blinding of hearts that turns people away from guidance; al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya keep the physical sense. On the transformation, Ibn Abbas says it means being turned into apes and swine, Abu Salih and al-Zamakhshari say stones, and al-Hasan and Qatada say being made immobile. Al-Razi reads the verse as a reply to the Qadariyya, showing that error occurs by God's will. Ibn Salam places the threat on the Day of Judgment, whereas most commentators understand it as applying in this world. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Ashur also explain that the punishment was not carried out because God did not will it.

The commentators explain that whoever We grant a long life, We return him in his creation to weakness and decline after strength and youth, until he reaches a state resembling that of a child, weak in body and lacking in reason and knowledge, like an arrow turned upside down. They read this as a call to reflect on the change in a person: if God can bring about this transformation, He can also resurrect the dead. Al-Tabari and al-Baghawi link the verse to the threat of transforming the disbelievers, while Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di mainly see in it proof that this world is a place of passage and not of permanence. Readers differ on the form of the verb (nunakkisuhu or nankusuhu) and on whether the final verb is in the third or second person. Al-Tabari prefers the intensive reading and the third person. On the general meaning, the commentators agree.

The commentators explain that this verse denies that the Prophet ﷺ was taught poetry, responding to those who called him a poet and called the Qur'an poetry. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others state that poetry is not fitting for his station and that what he brought is a reminder, an admonition and a clear Qur'an. According to al-Baghawi and others, some Quraysh, such as 'Uqba ibn Abi Mu'ayt in one report, made the claim. Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi relate that the pronoun 'him' refers to the Prophet, while Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Juzayy allow that it may refer to the Qur'an. The reports of verses the Prophet uttered, at Hunayn or while digging the trench, are explained by most as spoken without intent to rhyme or scan and therefore not poetry; al-Qurtubi cites al-Akhfash saying that 'I am the Prophet, no lie' is not a poem. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Ashur hold that unintended meter is not poetry, while others note that some poetry contains wisdom. As for 'to warn whoever is alive', Qatada and Ibn Kathir take it as life of heart and sight, al-Dahhak as sound reason, Yahya ibn Sallam as faith and al-Suddi as being guided. The readings 'linudhira' and 'litundhira' differ in whether the warning is attributed to the Qur'an or the Prophet. All agree that 'the word is fulfilled against the disbelievers' means punishment is due to them, while al-Zajjaj and al-Qurtubi note that the word may also mean proof.

This part of the verse states that the Qur'an the Prophet ﷺ brought is not poetry, as the polytheists claimed, that God did not teach him poetry and that it is not fitting for him, and that it is a reminder, an admonition and a clear Qur'an. Its purpose is to warn whoever is alive, meaning the sensible and thoughtful person who accepts the truth, and for the word of punishment to be due against the disbelievers who do not reflect. Commentators agree on this general meaning but differ on who is meant by 'the living'. Qatada says it is the one whose heart and sight are alive, al-Dahhak the one who has understanding, al-Suddi and Muqatil the one who is rightly guided in God's knowledge, Yahya ibn Sallam the believer, and al-Zajjaj the one who understands what is addressed to him. The reading varies between 'liyundhira' with a second-person verb, addressed to the Prophet, and a third-person verb, with the Qur'an as subject; al-Tabari holds both readings to be correct. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi take 'the word' to mean punishment, while al-Zamakhshari allows that it means punishment or proof. Al-Razi holds that the disbelievers are dead in reality though alive in appearance, whereas Ibn al-Qayyim stresses that punishment falls only after proof has been established. Several commentators note that rhythmic phrases that slipped from the Prophet, such as 'I am the Prophet, I do not lie', were not composed deliberately and so are not poetry, though others count them as verse.

This verse reminds the polytheists of God's favour: He created livestock for them, camels, cattle and sheep, by His power alone, without partner or helper, and made them owners of these animals. He also subdued them so that they ride some and eat from others, and they gain further benefits from their wool, hair and fur, and from their milk. Most commentators, such as Qatada, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Mahalli and al-Suyuti, explain 'owners' as 'able to control them'. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi read it as possession in the full sense of owners disposing of their property, with al-Zamakhshari combining both meanings. For 'Our hands', al-Hasan, al-Mawardi and Ibn Juzayy take it to mean power, while others, reported by al-Alusi, treat it as one of the ambiguous verses to be affirmed without interpretation. The readings differ on 'their riding', and al-Farra allowed the sense of a verbal noun. The commentators agree that the verse calls for gratitude and rebukes those who withhold it. The passage then turns to those who take gods besides God in hope of help, though these cannot help them. On 'a mobilised army', al-Hasan, Qatada and al-Zamakhshari understand the polytheists as defending their idols, while others take it to mean they will be gathered with them in the Fire.

This verse recalls that God created the grazing animals, camels, cattle and sheep, by His power alone, and made them serve people. He made them so docile that they can be ridden and loaded, and their meat can be eaten. The commentators agree that the verse lists blessings in order to establish the argument against the polytheists. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir explain that 'we subjected them' means 'we made them submissive', and that 'their riding' means what is ridden. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn al-Jawzi note that 'hands' stands for power, and that 'possessors' means 'those who control them', according to Qatada and others. Al-Razi argues that docility is an extra blessing, since a wild animal would be of little use. Al-Zamakhshari sees the attribution of the work to the hands as a metaphor that stresses God's sole creation. Readers differ on 'rakubuhum': most read it with a fatha, meaning what is ridden, while al-Hasan and al-A'mash read it with a damma as a verbal noun, and al-Farra' allowed that reading. Wool, hair and milk are the other benefits mentioned. The exegetes conclude that the verse calls for gratitude to the Creator and for affirming His oneness, and that it rebukes those who take other gods hoping for their help.

The commentators explain that God reminds the polytheists of His favours in the livestock, camels, cattle and sheep. He created them by His power, made them subject to human ownership, and tamed them so that people can ride some and eat their flesh. These animals also provide other benefits, such as wool, hair and fur, and milk to drink. For most exegetes, including al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi, the question "Will they not then be grateful?" is a rebuke to those who fail to give thanks, and gratitude means believing in the Giver, affirming His oneness and worshipping Him alone.

Opinions differ on some points. Al-Tabari, citing Qatada, takes the benefits to be wool and hair and the drinks to be milk. Al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi report that "possessing" means "controlling" according to Qatada and "being able to manage them" according to Ibn al-Sa'ib, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi see it as a possession granted by God. Al-Hasan takes "Our hands" to mean power, while al-Suddi takes it as direct action. Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi note that a child can lead a huge camel, illustrating how docile the animals are.

The commentators also discuss how to read the word for "their mount" and whether the idols are themselves an army or whether it is the polytheists who defend them. The views vary, and no clear consensus emerges. All agree, however, that these idols cannot help their worshippers.
