This verse says that the idolaters, after being given the blessings of the livestock, which Allah made subservient to them so that they ride them, eat from them, and drink their milk, took gods besides Allah, hoping that these would help them. The commentators agree that this hope is vain, since the idols cannot give them any support. On the phrase that they are an assembled host for them, opinions differ. Mujahid takes it to mean that they will be brought forward at the reckoning, al-Hasan that they will be brought into the Fire, and Qatada, as al-Tabari reports, that the polytheists become angry for their idols in this world while the idols bring them neither benefit nor protection. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir also report that the idols will be brought along with their worshippers into the Fire. Al-Zamakhshari relates the hope to intercession before Allah and holds that the reality is the reverse of what they imagined. All agree that the verse consoles the Prophet ﷺ regarding his opponents' words and warns them, since Allah knows what they conceal and what they disclose. Several scholars, including al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi, note that the particle translated as perhaps can be read in more than one grammatical way, but none of them decides between these readings.

This verse states that the idols which the polytheists took besides God cannot help their worshippers or protect them from punishment, so their hope in them is vain. Commentators differ on the phrase "and they are an assembled host for them." Al-Tabari, followed by Ibn Kathir, adopts the view of Qatada and al-Hasan that the disbelievers are a host for their idols in this world, becoming angry on their behalf, while the idols bring them neither benefit nor protection. Al-Mawardi reports from Mujahid that it means present at the reckoning. Al-Sam'ani, al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi mention the other reading, that the idols are an army for the worshippers, present with them in the Fire, or that the worshippers are gathered to serve and defend their idols. Al-Zamakhshari explains that the polytheists took these gods hoping for their support, but the reverse happens: they become fuel for the Fire. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Juzayy prefer the reading in which the unbelievers serve the idols in this life, which better conveys the shame they bring upon them.

The rest of the verse consoles the Prophet, peace be upon him, about his people's words, since God knows what they conceal and what they reveal. Al-Tabari says that envy drives them to these claims, because they know that what he brings is not poetry. Al-Razi offers several possible meanings of what they conceal and what they display, such as hypocrisy, associationism, or corrupt beliefs. Al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi note a reading with an open "anna", which grammarians take as causal. Ibn Kathir adds that everything will be exposed and recompensed on the Day of Judgment.

The commentators explain that this verse consoles the Prophet ﷺ and forbids him to grieve over the words of the polytheists about him: that he is a poet, a sorcerer, a soothsayer or a madman, and that he is not a messenger. God gives the reason as His knowledge of what they conceal and what they declare, and that He will repay them for it. The verse follows the statement that the idols they have taken cannot help them, and that they themselves are a host mustered for them. On the meaning of this 'host', opinions differ: al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Hasan, following Qatada, take it to mean that the disbelievers rage for their idols in this world, though the idols bring them neither good nor protection; Ibn Kathir adopts this reading and al-Tabari prefers it because the idols disown their worshippers on the Day of Reckoning. Mujahid takes it to mean that they will be brought forward at the reckoning, al-Hasan that they will be brought into the Fire, and Hamid that they will be summoned to defend them. Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi also report that the idols may be a host present with their worshippers in Hell. On what they 'conceal', al-Tabari takes it as their inner recognition of the truth of the message while they deny it aloud; al-Razi offers several readings: hypocrisy and polytheism, their knowledge of the Prophet alongside their open rejection, or corrupt beliefs and blameworthy deeds. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud treat God's knowledge as a figure for requital. The surrounding passages, which the commentators connect with this verse, argue for resurrection from the creation of man out of a drop of semen; these were revealed about a particular denier of resurrection, though the wording is generally applied to all who deny it. The readings also differ on 'yahzunak' (vowelling of the first letter) and on 'anna' (kasra or fatha), which the commentators discuss.

This passage affirms God's power to resurrect the dead by pointing to man's origin: created from a drop of semen, he becomes a manifest disputer who denies the Resurrection. The commentators agree on this general sense. They differ on who the denier was: al-Tabari reports it was Ubayy ibn Khalaf, al-'As ibn Wa'il, or Abd Allah ibn Ubayy, while Ibn Atiyya rejects the attribution to Ibn Abbas and Ibn Kathir notes that some of these reports are weak. The most widespread tradition says that this man brought a decayed bone, crumbled it in his hand and asked who would bring it back to life, and the Prophet replied that God would revive it, then send him to Hell.

Many exegetes, including Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi, take the phrase "man" in its generic sense, so the verse addresses every denier of resurrection. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi stress that God censures this denial: man was made from the basest matter, yet he dares to dispute with his Lord. Al-Razi observes that speech and understanding are more wondrous than the bodily form alone, which is why man is described as a manifest disputer.

The verse offers several arguments: the One who created man at the beginning can recreate him; the One who brings fire from the green tree can revive the dead; the One who created the heavens and earth can create the like of humans; and the command "Be!" suffices. Ibn Kathir also cites the Prophet's words on the dust of the body. These interpretations converge, while jurists debate the nature of bones, a point raised by al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi.

This verse from Surah Ya-Sin describes a denier of resurrection who took a decayed bone, crumbled it, and asked who could bring such bones back to life. The commentators explain that "he forgot his creation" means he forgot that he was made from a drop of semen; had he remembered, he would not have doubted being recreated. They agree that the answer given in the next verse is that the One who created them the first time can restore them, and He knows every creation. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that the man was Ubayy ibn Khalaf, while other reports name al-As ibn Wa'il or Abd Allah ibn Ubayy; Ibn 'Atiyya calls the latter attribution a mistake since the surah is Meccan, and Ibn Kathir holds that the verse applies to anyone who denies resurrection. The argument is reinforced by the fire struck from the green tree, by the creation of the heavens and earth, and by the command "Be, and it is". On a legal point, Abu Hanifa and some Shafi'is take the verse to show that bones are alive and thus become impure at death, whereas al-Shafi'i and others deny this; some read it as referring to the owners of the bones. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn al-'Arabi affirm that bones feel, while Ibn 'Ashur regards that feeling as slow. Al-Razi, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi follow the same line of reasoning, from the drop of fluid to the eloquent man.

This verse answers those who deny resurrection and find it hard to imagine bones reduced to dust being brought back to life. It says that the One who originated creation the first time can restore it, and that He knows every created thing, including scattered parts of bodies. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi, al-Baydawi and al-Alusi agree on this sense: restoration is easier than initial creation, and the argument rests on the plain evidence of the first creation.

The commentators relate that the verses were revealed concerning a man, named in the reports as Ubayy ibn Khalaf, al-As ibn Wa'il or Abu Jahl, who brought Muhammad a crumbling bone, broke it and asked whether God could revive it. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Attiya note that the sura is Meccan, which makes the attribution to Abd Allah ibn Ubayy doubtful, and they hold that the verse applies to everyone who denies resurrection, since al-insan is generic. Ibn Attiya observes that the definite form may still point to a particular person.

There is a legal disagreement over the bone. Abu Hanifa and some followers of al-Shafi'i, as al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi report, conclude that bones carry life and become impure at death. Al-Shafi'i and others, according to al-Qurtubi, deny that life inhabits bone and read "the bones" as meaning their owners, or as the restoration of bones to their former state. Al-Alusi finds the first reading more apparent while noting the debate. Secondary arguments, such as the green wood from which fire comes, which Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain through the marikh and afar trees, or the creation of the heavens and earth, show that God brings forth opposites from one another.

The commentators agree that the reasoning moves from the greater to the lesser: the One who created the heavens and the earth can recreate human beings. Ibn al-Qayyim sees in these verses a complete proof resting on God's knowledge, power and sovereignty.

This verse, within the response to those who deny resurrection and find it impossible to revive decayed bones, states that the One who produced fire for you from a green tree is able to recreate you. Commentators explain that the green tree most often means the markh and the ifar, two woods from which fire is struck by rubbing one against the other; Ibn Abbas holds that nearly every tree contains fire, except the ʿunnab, while al-Kalbi and the sages extend it to all trees. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others agree that the argument rests on the production of opposites: greenness signals moisture and water, whereas fire is hot and dry, so the One who brings fire from wet wood can restore life to bones. Commentators connect the verse to the denial of resurrection and differ on who was meant, with al-As ibn Wa'il and Ubayy ibn Khalaf named most often, though Ibn Kathir treats the verse as general in application. Al-Qurtubi, al-Nasafi and Ibn Juzayy observe that the collective word shajar may be treated as masculine or feminine, and that the reading al-khadra follows the sense. The following verses, which argue that the Creator of the heavens and earth can create people like them, complete the reasoning.

This verse of Surah Ya-Sin asks whether the One who created the heavens and the earth is not able to create the like of human beings, that is, to bring them back after death. God answers Himself with "Yes", for He is the Creator and the All-Knowing. The commentators agree on the core sense: the creation of the vast heavens and earth is greater than the creation of humans, so the One who made the greater can remake the lesser. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn Juzayy and Ibn Ashur take "their like" to mean human beings, while al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi understand it as creatures smaller than the heavens and the earth, or as the resurrection itself. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn al-Qayyim connect the verse to the question of the decayed bones, and Ibn al-Qayyim draws out several proofs from it. Most exegetes read the verse as evidence for the bodily resurrection. Ya'qub's reading "yaqdiru" in the verb form is noted by Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan. Several commentators, including al-Qurtubi and al-Suyuti, report that the verse was revealed about a man who crumbled an old bone before the Prophet, though they do not agree on his identity, and they hold that this story does not limit the general meaning of the verse. Some exegetes take the pronoun to refer to the heavens and earth, but the more common view is that it refers to humans.

The commentators explain that the verse describes how God acts when He wills something: He says to it "Be" and it is immediately. It concludes the argument for resurrection that precedes it. God, they note, who created the fire from the green tree and the heavens and earth, which are greater than humankind, can revive decayed bones; his command is as swift as a glance. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi agree that the point is the speed and ease with which God creates, needing no tool, effort or helper.

They differ on the nature of the word "Be". Many early scholars, as al-Alusi reports, take it as an actual spoken word. Others, including al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud, read it as a figure of speech that conveys the power of God through the analogy of an obeyed commander. al-Razi discusses at length whether the divine will and speech are eternal or temporal, a question he treats as theologically contested. On the reading, Ibn 'Amir and al-Kisa'i read "fayakuna" in the subjunctive, linking it to "yaqul", while most readers use the indicative as an independent clause.

Finally, "malakut kulli shay'" is glossed by al-Tabari as the ownership of everything and its treasuries, by al-Mawardi as the treasuries of everything or its sovereignty with emphasis, and by Ibn Kathir as having the same sense as "mulk". The verse ends by recalling that all will return to God.

In this verse God declares His own glory and absolute transcendence above what the disbelievers attribute to Him, affirming that He alone holds the sovereignty of everything, governs it by His power, and that all people will be returned to Him after death for judgment. The verse closes the surah's argument for resurrection. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud explain that malakut means complete sovereignty, the added waw and ta' serving to intensify the meaning. Al-Mawardi offers a second reading, namely the treasuries of everything. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya take the verse as a proof of the bodily resurrection, while al-Razi sees in it both the affirmation of divine unity and the affirmation of the gathering on the Last Day. Al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi report variant readings such as malaka and mamlaka, which do not greatly change the meaning. Ibn Kathir distinguishes between the realm of bodies, al-mulk, and the realm of spirits, al-malakut, but he accepts the first view as the majority opinion. Several commentators cite hadiths praising the virtues of Surah Ya-Sin, but most note weaknesses in their chains of transmission and do not rely on them to explain the verse. The return to God, according to most scholars, takes place on the Day of Resurrection, and Ya'qub reads the verb with an open ta'.
